claim: The article's title claim -- that over 50% of creators earn less than $15,000 a year -- is not sourced anywhere in the article body; no study, survey, or dataset is cited for this specific figure.
stance_target: Whether the '50%+ earn under $15,000/year' statistic has a traceable evidentiary basis
scope_conditions: No source cited anywhere in the piece for this headline number; the only traceable adjacent figure in the piece (Linktree's 12% earning over $50K) does not itself establish the '50%+ under $15,000' claim
quoted_support: If over 50% of creators relied solely on their annual earnings from content creation, they would not only be homeless, they would probably die of starvation.
region: US framing (median pay comparator in USD); not Southeast Asia specific

claim: A Linktree survey of 9,500 creators found only 12% earn more than $50,000 a year, the one figure in this article with a traceable named origin.
stance_target: A large majority of creators do not reach full-time-equivalent income levels
scope_conditions: Linktree Creator Report, a self-selected vendor survey of Linktree's own userbase (n=9,500); not a random or representative sample of all content creators
quoted_support: A Linktree survey of 9,500 Creators revealed only 12% of them earn more than 50K a year.
time_period: Undated in this secondary source (Linktree Creator Report)
region: Likely US/Western given Linktree's userbase skew; not stated

claim: The article asserts YouTube has a Gini coefficient of 0.89 for creator income, higher than the most unequal nations on earth, with the top 5% of creators capturing 90% of income, the next 15% capturing 9%, and the bottom 80% capturing 1% -- but no computation, dataset, or citation supports this figure anywhere in the piece.
stance_target: Magnitude of income inequality among content creators (unverified precise figure)
scope_conditions: No source, computation, or dataset given; comparison nations' own Gini figures are also unsourced and one (UAE) is corrupted to a bare '.' in the source text, suggesting a copy-paste error that further undermines confidence in the surrounding numbers
quoted_support: YouTube has a Gini Coefficient of 0.89. This is higher than the most unequal countries on Earth, including South Africa, Brazil, and the United Arab Emirates, which have a Gini Score of .82, .81 and . respectively.
region: Global comparison framing (South Africa, Brazil, UAE); not Southeast Asia specific

claim: The article names a $15,000/year 'Survival Barrier' and $50,000/year 'Full-Time Barrier' as two thresholds creator income distributions cluster below, and offers an economic (not motivational) mechanism for attrition: creators below the barrier must hold a second job, reducing production time and lengthening time-to-breakthrough, increasing the likelihood of quitting.
stance_target: Documented reasons creators give for quitting include the economic bind of needing a second job while below a monetization threshold, which itself delays reaching that threshold
scope_conditions: Conceptual framing, not empirically measured in this piece; presented as the author's own analytical framework
quoted_support: If you are one of the creators who has yet to break the barrier, you most likely have to work a 9-5 in order to pay the bills. This means less time devoted to creating content... this means a higher likelihood that they will either quit or get talked into quitting by their loved ones.

claim: The article claims the percentage of creators earning under $15,000/year increased by 2.61% since 2023 even as the creator economy grew by over 19%, a precise two-decimal-point figure presented with no survey or dataset cited.
stance_target: Aggregate market growth does not translate into broad-based creator income gains ('growth lifts all boats' is false)
scope_conditions: No source given for either the 2.61 percentage-point change or the 19% industry growth figure
quoted_support: The percentage of creators earning under $15,000 has increased by 2.61% since 2023, even as the industry grew by over 19%.
region: Not specified; US framing implied by other figures in the piece

claim: The article states US median pay is $58,084/year as its living-wage comparator, against which its unsourced $15,000 'Survival Barrier' represents roughly a quarter.
stance_target: Living-wage benchmark used for comparison in this piece
scope_conditions: US median pay figure, source not cited in this secondary article
quoted_support: To put this into perspective, typical U.S median pay is $58,084 a year. $15K a year is roughly a quarter of that, and is certainly not enough to get by.
